facts.text: An owl can turn its head as far as 270 degrees in either direction.
That is more than twice as far as a human can safely turn the head.
Owl eyes are shaped like tubes rather than balls and are fixed in their sockets, so owls cannot move their eyes the way people do.
Because their eyes cannot move, owls have to turn their whole head to look around.
Owls have 14 neck bones (vertebrae), twice as many as the 7 in a human neck.
In humans, a sudden twist of the neck can stretch or tear the arteries that carry blood to the brain, and this can lead to a stroke.
A team from Johns Hopkins University, led by medical illustrator Fabian de Kok-Mercado, studied why owls are not hurt by turning their heads.
The team examined 12 owls of three kinds (snowy, barred and great horned owls) that had died of natural causes.
The researchers injected dye into the birds' blood vessels, turned the heads by hand, and used X-ray pictures (CT scans and angiography) to see the blood flow.
In owls, the holes in the neck bones that the main arteries pass through are about 10 times wider than the arteries, which leaves room for the arteries to move.
Not all of an owl's neck arteries run through the bones.
Just below an owl's jaw, some blood vessels get bigger as blood flows in, and the extra blood collects there like small reservoirs.
Human arteries, in contrast, tend to get narrower when the head turns.
Small vessels connect the main arteries of an owl's neck, so blood can keep reaching the brain even when the head is turned far.
A poster about the findings won first place in the 2012 International Science and Engineering Visualization Challenge.
